questions.text:
Read the following article and answer the questions.

	In the mid 19th century, Dr Semmelweiss came to work in a hospital. He noticed that many women whose babies were delivered by doctors died from infections, but this was not the case when deliveries were done by midwives. He also observed that the doctors were going straight from dissecting dead bodies to delivering babies. He wondered if the doctors were carrying the cause of the infections from the dead bodies to the women.
	In a controlled experiment, he made doctors wash their hands before delivering babies. Immediately, the death rate dropped sharply. Dr Semmelweiss presented his findings to other doctors but his ideas were not accepted at that time. It was hard for doctors to admit that they might have passed the infections and killed their patients.	

a	What was the observation that led to Dr Semmelweiss's investigation?															(1 mark)
b	What hypothesis did Dr Semmelweiss propose to explain the observation in a?													(1 mark)
c	Why did Dr Semmelweiss include hand-washing in his experimental  design?												(1 mark)
d	State two reasons why Dr Semmelweiss's ideas were not immediately accepted.												(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	More women died from infections when deliveries were done by doctors. Fewer 			women died when deliveries were done by midwives.				1m
	b	Doctors carried the cause of the infections from the dead bodies to the women. 																1m
	c	To eliminate the cause of infections picked up from dead bodies. 		1m
	d	Doctors could not admit that they might have passed the infections and killed their 		patients. /
		Hand-washing was a strange idea at that time. /
		Many doctors thought that the infections were God's punishment to the women.
	 	(any 2 or other reasonable answers)							1m x 2

questions.text:
Peter observed that there were many metal sticks on the ground near a tree. He looked up and noticed that a nest was built on the tree. Based on the observation, he proposed a hypothesis to explain the appearance of the metal sticks.
a	What is a hypothesis?									(1 mark)
b	Suggest a hypothesis based on Peter's observations.			(2 marks)
c	Describe an experiment that can be done to confirm the hypothesis in b.															(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	A hypothesis is a reasonable answer to the question about the observations.																	1m
	b	Birds use metal sticks to build their nests and the metal sticks drop from the nests.																2m
	c	Make a mark on some metal sticks. 								1m
		Put the marked metal sticks in a place where the birds can reach. 		1m
		If the marked metal sticks are found in the nest and on the ground, the hypothesis 		is supported. 												1m

questions.text: Briefly contrast organisms and non-living things. 				(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Organisms can produce offspring but non-living things cannot.				1m
	Organisms obtain food for energy, growth and maintaining health but non-living things 	do not.														1m
	Organisms break down food to release stored energy for various body activities but 	non-living things do not.											1m
	Organisms increase in size and in complexity but non-living things do not. 		1m
	Organisms remove waste products produced from chemical reactions in their bodies but 	non-living things do not.											1m
	Organisms can detect changes in their environment and make responses but non-living 	things cannot.													1m
	Most animals can move freely from place to place and plants can move by growing but 	non-living things cannot move.										1m
	Communication													3m

questions.text: Describe the steps commonly involved in a scientific investigation.	(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Firstly, observations are made.										1m
	A question about the observations is then raised.							1m
	A reasonable answer to the question (hypothesis) is suggested.				1m
	Based on the hypothesis, a prediction is made.							1m
	The hypothesis is tested by doing experiments.							1m
	Control set-ups are often prepared to ensure the results of the experiments are due only 	to the factors under investigation.									1m
	A conclusion is drawn based on the results of the experiment. 				1m
	Communication													3m

questions.text: Describe the procedures of using a light microscope to observe a prepared slide under high-power magnification.								(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Insert a low-power eyepiece into the body tube and select a low-power objective.																		1m
Turn on the light source. Look through the eyepiece and adjust the diaphragm until the light is sufficient.												1m
Clip the prepared slide onto the stage.								1m
Watch the stage from the side and raise the stage by turning the coarse adjustment knob until the objective is at a position closest to the slide. 					1m
Look through the eyepiece and lower the stage by turning the coarse adjustment knob until the image is roughly in focus.									1m
Turn the fine adjustment knob to get a sharp focus.						1m
Move the part of the specimen you want to observe in detail to the centre of the field of view.															1m
Rotate the nosepiece to select a high-power objective. Turn the fine adjustment knob to get a sharp focus.												1m
Adjust the diaphragm to brighten the view if necessary.					1m
Communication													3m

questions.topic: Ch3 · Movement of substances across cell membrane
questions.text: State three ways in which osmosis is different from diffusion.		(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
Osmosis always involves a differentially permeable membrane while diffusion does not.															1m
Osmosis refers to the movement of water molecules only, while diffusion refers to the movement of any molecules including water molecules.					1m
During osmosis, there is a net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (i.e. lower solute concentration) to a region of lower water potential 
(i.e. higher solute concentration). During diffusion, there is a net movement of molecules from a region of higher solute concentration to a region of lower solute concentration.																1m

questions.topic: Ch3 · Movement of substances across cell membrane
questions.text:
a	Chloride ions cannot diffuse across the cell membrane directly. With reference to the structure of the cell membrane illustrated by the fluid mosaic model, explain why. 								(2 marks)
b	Cholera is a disease caused by a bacterium. The bacterium releases a toxin which causes chloride ions to move from the epithelial cells lining the inner wall of the intestine to the lumen. This results in diarrhoea. The patient produces a large amount of watery faeces. 
i	Explain why the movement of chloride ions from the epithelial cells to the lumen of the intestine results in diarrhoea. 			(3 marks)

Diarrhoea patients can drink a solution called oral rehydration solution to help recovery. The solution contains glucose, salts and water. Glucose and salts in the solution help the absorption of water in the intestine. 
ii	Describe how the glucose and salts in the oral rehydration solution help the absorption of water in the intestine.				(2 marks)
iii	Sports drinks also contain glucose, salts and water, but the concentration of glucose is usually higher than that in oral rehydration solution. Explain why drinking sports drinks cannot help the recovery of diarrhoea patients and may even make diarrhoea worse. 	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	The cell membrane is composed of a phospholipid bilayer. 				1m
Chloride ions are charged / hydrophilic. They are repelled by the phospholipid bilayer.													1m
b	i	As the chloride ions move to the lumen, the water potential in the lumen becomes lower. 										1m 
This causes water to move from the epithelial cells to the lumen by osmosis.													1m
The intestine of the patients does not absorb water / absorbs only a small amount of water, thus a large amount of watery faeces is produced. 	1m
ii	Glucose and salts in the oral rehydration solution are absorbed into the epithelial cells.											1m
This lowers the water potential of the epithelial cells. Water in the lumen of the intestine then enters the epithelial cells by osmosis.			1m
iii	After drinking sports drinks, the high concentration of glucose lowers the water potential in the lumen of the intestine.					1m
This causes water to move from the epithelial cells to the lumen by osmosis, making diarrhoea worse. 									1m

questions.topic: Ch3 · Movement of substances across cell membrane
questions.text: Using suitable examples, discuss the importance of diffusion, osmosis and active transport to organisms.										(12 marks)
questions.answerText:

and the absorption of water in plant roots are carried out by osmosis. 			1m

questions.text:
a	State, with one example, what physical digestion is.			(3 marks)
b	Using the digestion of lipids as an example, explain the difference of physical digestion and chemical digestion.					(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	Physical digestion is the breaking down of food into smaller pieces by physical actions.													1m
It increases the surface area of food.								1m
Example: chewing in the mouth cavity / mastication / churning in the stomach / emulsification of lipids by bile salts								1m
b	Emulsification of lipids is a kind of physical digestion. The bile salts in the bile emulsify lipids into small droplets.								1m
It involves no enzymes and the chemical structure of lipids does not change.															1m
Breaking down of lipids into fatty acids and glycerol in the small intestine is a kind of chemical digestion. 										1m
It is a chemical reaction in which large, complex lipid molecules are broken down into small, soluble forms. It is catalysed by the enzyme pancreatic lipase. 	1m

questions.text:
Microscopy has enabled extensive study of the tissue layers of the ileum. Describe the structure and function of each of the tissue layers of the ileum.															(9 marks)
						CCEA GCE (AS) Biology Unit AS 1 May 2018 Q8b
questions.answerText:
Villi are present on the inner wall of the ileum. This increases the surface area for absorption.													1m
Epithelial cells of the villi have a large number of microvilli. This increases the surface area for absorption.												1m
There are many mitochondria in the epithelial cells. This provides energy for active transport of food molecules.										1m
Villi have a rich network of capillaries which maintains a steep concentration gradient of food molecules between the lumen and the blood.						1m
Lacteal is present in the villi for the absorption of lipids and lipid-soluble food molecules.															1m
The circular and longitudinal muscles contract alternatively (peristalsis). This brings the digested food molecules into close contact with the villi for absorption.			1m
(or other reasonable answers)
Communication													3m

questions.text: Compare and contrast how starch in potato and proteins in egg white are digested in the human digestive system. 								(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Both potato and egg white are broken down into smaller pieces physically during mastication in the mouth cavity.										1m
Both potato and egg white are broken down into smaller pieces physically during churning in the stomach. 											1m
Starch in potato is digested into maltose by the salivary amylase from the saliva in the mouth cavity, while proteins in the egg white are not.						1m
Proteins in egg white are digested into peptides by the pepsin from the gastric juice in the stomach, while starch in the potato is not.							1m
The remaining starch in potato is digested into maltose by the pancreatic amylase from the pancreatic juice in duodenum.									1m
The maltose is further digested into glucose by the maltase in the cell membrane of the specialized cells in the epithelium of the small intestine.					1m
Peptides from egg white are further digested into amino acids by the proteases from the pancreatic juice in the duodenum and proteases in the cell membrane of the specialized cells in the epithelium of the small intestine. 							1m
Communication		 											3m

questions.text: Describe the structural adaptations of villi for the absorption of food molecules. Explain why people with a breakdown of villi sometimes suffer from deficiency diseases.													(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Structural adaptations of villi:
Villi are finger-like projections. They increase the surface area for absorption. 	1m
The epithelium of villi is very thin / only one-cell thick. This provides a short distance for diffusion of food molecules into the blood and lymph. 						1m
The cell membrane of the epithelial cells of the villi has a large number of microvilli / brush borders. This increases the surface area for absorption. 				1m
Villi have lacteals and capillaries. They allow the absorbed food molecules to be carried away rapidly, thus keeping a steep concentration gradient to increase the rate of diffusion. 														1m
Effect of breakdown of villi:
Breakdown of villi reduces the surface area for absorption of different food molecules.																1m
Some food molecules cannot be absorbed and are lost.					1m
Without adequate amounts of nutrients, deficiency diseases may develop.		1m
Communication													3m

questions.text: Describe how lipids are digested and absorbed and describe the fate of the absorbed lipids in our body.									(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
The process of digestion and absorption: 
Physical actions such as chewing in the mouth cavity and churning in the stomach break down the food into smaller pieces. /
In the duodenum, bile salts in the bile emulsify lipids into small droplets. /
This facilitates chemical digestion of the lipids by increasing the surface area for lipases to act on. /
Pancreatic lipase in the pancreatic juice catalyses the breakdown of emulsified lipids into fatty acids and glycerol. /
Fatty acids and glycerol enter the epithelial cells of the villi in the ileum by diffusion. /
They recombine into fine lipids droplets in the epithelial cells. /
Lipids enter the lymph in the lacteals. /
Lipids are transported to the main lymph vessels and then to bloodstream near the neck region. They are then carried to all parts of the body. (any 5)			1m x 5
The fate of absorbed lipids:
The absorbed lipids act as energy reserves in the body. / 
They are stored in adipose tissues in our body. /
They can be used by cells to make cell membranes. / 
They can be used to make hormones. (any 2)						1m x 2
Communication 											3m

questions.text: Explain how the structure of the walls of the stomach and ileum is related to their functions.													(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Stomach:
Muscles are present in the stomach wall. /
The muscles contract to churn the food. /
This increases the surface area of food for chemical digestion. /
Gastric glands are present on the stomach wall. /
Gastric glands produce gastric juice for chemical digestion. /
Gastric juice contains mucus, which protects the stomach wall from being digested and damaged. (any 4)											1m x 4
Ileum:
The inner wall of the ileum is highly folded. / 
Many finger-like projections / villi are present on the inner wall. /
The cell membrane of the epithelial cells of the villi has a large number of microvilli / brush borders. / 
These features increase the surface area for absorption. /	
The epithelium of villi is very thin / only one-cell thick. / 
This provides a short distance for diffusion of food molecules into the blood and lymph. / 
Villi have lacteals and capillaries. /
They allow the absorbed food molecules to be carried away rapidly, thus keeping a steep concentration gradient to increase the rate of diffusion. /
Muscles in the wall of the ileum contract and relax alternatively to produce wave-like movement. This movement brings food molecules into close contact with the villi. / 
This helps keep a steep concentration gradient to increase the rate of diffusion. 
(any 4)													1m x 4
Communication												3m

questions.text: Explain why oxygen in the air sacs can enter the red blood cells in the blood efficiently.												(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Any seven from: 											1m x 7
A large number of air sacs are present in the lungs. This provides a very large surface area for the diffusion of oxygen.
The walls of the air sacs and the capillaries are one-cell thick. This reduces the diffusion distance of oxygen. 
The inner surfaces of air sacs are lined with a film of water. This allows oxygen in inhaled air to dissolve in the water film and diffuse across the walls of the air sacs. 
Air sacs are richly supplied with capillaries. This allows rapid transport of oxygen away from the air sacs. Therefore a steep concentration gradient of oxygen between the air sacs and the blood can be maintained for efficient diffusion of oxygen. 
The walls of air sacs are in close contact with capillaries. This reduces the diffusion distance of oxygen. 
Red blood cells are in a biconcave disc shape. This provides a large surface area to volume ratio for the diffusion of oxygen into the cells. 
The biconcave disc shape of red blood cells also provides a short distance for oxygen to reach the haemoglobin in the red blood cells rapidly. 
Red blood cells are fully packed with haemoglobin which is an excellent oxygen carrier. 
Mature red blood cells have no nucleus. This provides more room for holding haemoglobin.
Communication												3m

The movements increase the volume of the thoracic cavity, and hence the volume of the lungs.														1m
The air pressure in the lungs decreases and becomes lower than the atmospheric pressure.														1m
Air rushes into the lungs through the respiratory tract.						1m
Communication													3m

questions.topic: Ch10 · Transpiration, transport and support in plants
questions.text:

b	Explain why adding too much fertilizers to the soil may be harmful to the plant.												(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	As water is drawn up the xylem vessels by transpiration pull, water in the cortex cells near the xylem vessels of the roots enters the xylem vessels.		1m
The water potentials of these cortex cells decrease. Water is drawn from the adjacent cells by osmosis.										1m
As a result, a water potential gradient is set up across the cortex of the roots. Water moves inwards from cell to cell by osmosis, or moves inwards along the cell walls.													1m
Water potentials of root hair cells become lower than the water potential of the soil. Water in the soil enters the root hair cells by osmosis.					1m
b	Adding fertilizers lowers the water potential of the soil water.			1m
The water potential of the soil water becomes lower than that of the root hair cells. 														1m
Therefore water cannot enter the root by osmosis. This may cause the plant to dehydrate.													1m

a	Clean the roots of several herbaceous plants with water. Do not damage the roots.														1m

b	Water vapour evaporates from the mesophyll cells around the air spaces.	1m
Water is drawn from the adjacent cells by osmosis. As a result, a water potential gradient is set up across the leaf.								1m
Water is finally drawn from the xylem vessels.						1m
This creates a force to pull water up the xylem vessels.				1m
The continuous hollow tube-like structure of xylem vessels allows water to be carried up as a continuous stream of water.							1m

Water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells near the air spaces.	1m
Water is drawn from the adjacent cells by osmosis. As a result, a water potential gradient is set up across the leaves.									1m
Water is finally drawn from the xylem vessels.							1m

questions.topic: Ch10 · Transpiration, transport and support in plants
questions.text:
Plants absorb water from the soil via their roots.
Describe the pathways and mechanisms by which water passes from the soil to the xylem vessels in the root.									(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
In the leaves, mesophyll cells near the air spaces lose water continuously into the air spaces.														1m
This creates transpiration pull. Water is drawn up the xylem vessels from the roots to the leaves.														1m
Water in the cortex cells near the xylem vessels of the roots enters the xylem vessels.																1m
The water potentials of these cortex cells decrease. Water is drawn from the neighbouring cells by osmosis.										1m
As a result, a water potential gradient is set up across the cortex of the roots.	1m
Water moves from cell to cell along a water potential gradient by osmosis		1m
through the cytoplasm and the vacuoles of cells.							1m
Water also moves travels from one cell to another freely through the cell wall.	1m
The water potentials of the root hair cells become lower than that of the soil. Water in the soil enters the root hair cells by osmosis.								1m
Communication													3m

questions.topic: Ch10 · Transpiration, transport and support in plants
questions.text: A rose and a tulip were put in a glass without water. After an hour the tulip stalk bent but the rose stalk remained upright. Explain.					(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
The two flowers lost water due to transpiration.							1m
The cells in the cortex and pith of their stems became flaccid.				1m
The stalk of tulip was mainly supported by the turgidity of cells in the cortex and pith.																1m
As the cells became flaccid, they could no longer support the stalk.			1m
The stalk of rose was mainly supported by the rigidity of xylem.				1m
The cell walls of xylem vessels contain lignin, which are hard and rigid.		1m
This physical nature is independent of the water content of the plant.			1m
Communication													3m

questions.text:
The diploid number of an organism is 28. Which of the following comparisons between a diploid cell and a haploid cell of the organism is correct?

B	It contains 28 sets of chromosomes.	It contains 14 sets of chromosomes.	
C	It contains homologous chromosomes.	It contains non-homologous chromosomes only.	
D	It contains both maternal and paternal chromosomes.	It contains maternal chromosomes only.

Which of the following events occurs first in meiotic cell division?
A	lining up of homologous chromosomes along the equator
B	formation of chiasmata
	C	separation of members of each pair of homologous chromosomes
D	formation of new nuclear membrane

What is the significance of formation of chiasmata in cell division?
A	It results in independent assortment of chromosomes.
B	It halves the number of chromosomes.

D	It allows the exchange of genetic material in a pair of homologous chromosomes.

Which of the following is/are the correct comparison(s) of mitosis and meiosis?

	(2)	Crossing over occurs in both mitosis and meiosis.

A	(1) only					B	(1) and (2) only

	B	(1) and (2) only

Which of the following processes involve(s) mitotic cell division?

	(2)	Some cells in the skin divide to produce new cells to replace the dead ones.
	(3)	Some cells in the root tip grow in size to increase the length of the root.

B	(1) and (2) only
	C	(2) and (3) only		
D	(1), (2) and (3)

A	The two members of each pair of homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles of the cell.

Which of the following events does not take place during interphase of a cell cycle?

	(2)	ovary
	(3)	bone marrow

B	(1) and (2) only
	C	(2) and (3) only		
D	(1), (2) and (3)

Which of the following statements correctly state(s) the importance for reducing the chromosome number during meiotic cell division?

(2)	It reduces genetic variations in the offspring.
(3)	It provides a larger number of cells for reproduction.

B	(2) only
	C	(1) and (2) only
D	(1), (2) and (3)

Which of the following events occur only in meiotic cell division but not in mitotic cell division?
(1)	replication of DNA
(2)	separation of homologous chromosomes
(3)	formation of chiasmata between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
A	(1) and (2) only			B	(1) and (3) only
C	(2) and (3) only			D	(1), (2) and (3)

Which of the following statements about interphase of the cell cycle is incorrect?
A	Genetic material replicates during interphase.
B	Chromosomes are visible under the light microscope during interphase.
C	Cellular metabolism is extraordinarily active during interphase.
D	Interphase occupies the majority of time in a cell cycle.

Anaphase I in meiosis is different from anaphase in mitosis, because anaphase I involves
A	replication of chromosomes to form sister chromatids.
B	replication of chromosomes to form homologous pairs.
C	separation of sister chromatids which then move to opposite poles of the cell.
D	separation of homologous chromosomes which then move to opposite poles of the cell.

Which of the following statements about mitotic cell division and meiotic cell division is incorrect?
A	Mitotic cell division occurs in body cells.
B	Mitotic cell division forms cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
C	Meiotic cell division occurs in gametes.
D	Meiotic cell division forms cells for sexual reproduction.

If the amount of DNA in a body cell of an organism at prophase of cell division is 1 unit, what is the amount of DNA in a sperm of this organism?
A	1 unit				B	1/2 unit
C	1/3 unit				D	1/4 unit

Which of the following statements about the second meiotic division is correct?
A	Independent assortment of chromosomes occurs.
B	Pairing of homologous chromosomes occurs.
C	Each chromosome consists of a pair of chromatids during prophase II.
D	Chromosomes become visible at the end of telophase II.

Before mitosis, a plant cell produces
A	a thicker cell wall.			B	more DNA.
C	less cytoplasm.			D	more nuclei.

What will be formed from the meiotic cell division of a cell?
A	two new cells which are genetically identical
B	two new cells which are genetically different 
C	four new cells which are genetically identical
D	four new cells which are genetically different

Which of the following statements about chromosomes is correct?
A	Chromosomes of the same size and shape in a cell may carry different genetic information.
B	Two chromosomes join together to form a chromatid.
C	All animal cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes.
D	All chromosomes consist of two identical DNA molecules.

Which of the following is not the significance of mitotic cell division?
A	It is important for the growth of plants and animals.
B	It produces new cells to replace the damaged ones.
C	It allows some organisms to produce offspring by asexual reproduction.
D	It enables some species of organisms to have genetic variations.

Independent assortment is important in meiotic cell division because
A	it limits the variations of genetic information in gametes.
B	it halves the number of chromosomes in gametes.
C	it produces different combinations of genetic information in gametes.
D	it preserves the number of chromosomes from generation to generation.

Which of the following are not daughter cells of meiotic cell division?

(2)	skin cells
(3)	red blood cells
A	(3) only
B	(1) and (2) only 
C	(2) and (3) only
D	(1), (2) and (3)

questions.answerText:

During prophase, the a                      breaks down and

questions.text: Give an account of mitotic cell division which includes mitosis and cytokinesis.															(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Mitosis:
Mitosis is the nuclear division of mitotic cell division. /
During prophase, chromosomes shorten and thicken. They become visible. /
Each chromosome is seen to consist of two chromatids joined at the centromere. /
The nuclear membrane breaks down. /
During metaphase, the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell. /
During anaphase, the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate and move to the opposite poles of the cell. /
During telophase, new nuclear membranes form around each group of chromosomes. /
The chromosomes uncoil to become chromatin again. They become invisible. 
(any 6)													1m x 6
Cytokinesis:
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm of the parent cell into two equal halves. 															1m
In animal cells, the cell membrane constricts inwards until the cell separates into two. 															1m
In plant cells, a cell plate made up of new cell walls and cell membranes is formed between two nuclei.											1m
Communication												3m

questions.text: Describe the events that occur in meiotic cell division and explain the importance of meiotic cell division to organisms.							(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Events in the first meiotic division: 
DNA replicates. /
Each chromosome consists of two chromatids. /
Members of each pair of homologous chromosomes pair up. /
The nuclear membrane breaks down. /
Crossing over may occur between non-sister chromatids in pairs of homologous chromosomes. /
Homologous pairs line up along the equator. /
Independent assortment occurs. /
The two members of each homologous pair separate and move to opposite poles of the cell. /
New nuclear membranes form around each group of chromosomes.
(any 4)													1m x 4
Events in the second meiotic division: 
The nuclear membranes break down again. /
Chromosomes line up along the equator. /
The sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cells. /
New nuclear membranes form around each group of chromosomes. /
After cytoplasmic division, four haploid daughter cells are formed. (any 3) 	1m x 3
Importance of meiotic cell division:
Meiotic cell division produces haploid gametes for sexual reproduction.	1m
It produces genetic variations in gametes.							1m
Communication												3m

Date palm trees

questions.text: Explain the importance of seed and fruit dispersal and describe three different methods of it.												(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Importance of seed and fruit dispersal:
Seed and fruit dispersal can reduce overcrowding and competition for resources (e.g. water, light, nutrients and space) among the daughter and parent plants.	1m
It allows the species to colonize new areas.							1m
The daughter plants can escape from pests and diseases associated with the parent plants.													1m
Methods of seed and fruit dispersal: 
Some seeds are dispersed by explosion. Tension in the fruit wall increases as the pod dries up. This causes the pod to split open and release the seeds inside. /
Some seeds are light and may have 'parachutes'. They can be dispersed by wind. /
Some fruits are buoyant and can be dispersed by water currents. /
Some fruits are brightly coloured and juicy to attract animals to eat them. Their seeds are dispersed when they pass out in the faeces of the animals. /
Some seeds have hooks. They can cling to the hairs of animals. They are carried away from the parent plant and dispersed when the animals move. 
(any 3)													2m x 3
Communication												3m

questions.text: Describe how an insect-pollinated flower is adapted to its functions.	(11 marks)

The petals are large and brightly coloured. They often have nectar guide and are scented to attract insects. /
The anthers are located inside the flower and firmly attached to the filaments. When insects obtain nectar, pollen grains attach to the insects. / 
The stigma is broad and sticky to pick up pollen grains from insects. /
The pollen grains produced are rough and sticky to help attach to the insects. / 
Nectaries are present to secrete nectar to attract insects. 
(any 4) 													2m x 4
Communication												3m

questions.text: Describe how the eye and the ear of humans detect stimulus. Give an account of how the structures of the eye and the ear are adapted for detecting stimuli.																(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
The eye is the sense organ for detecting light. The ear is the sense organ for detecting sound. 														1m
In the eye, the cornea, aqueous humour, lens and vitreous humour are transparent. They are responsible for refracting light rays that enter the eye. 				1m
Light rays are focused on the retina, where light-sensitive cells (rod cells and cone cells) are located. 													1m
When the light-sensitive cells are stimulated by light, they send nerve impulses to the brain through the optic nerve for interpretation. 							1m
In the ear, sound waves are collected by pinna. 							1m
The sound waves cause the eardrum to vibrate. 							1m
Ear bones are responsible for amplifying and transmitting the vibrations. 		1m
When the vibrations reach the fluids in the cochlea, sensory hair cells are stimulated. 																	1m
The sensory hair cells send nerve impulses to the brain through the auditory nerve for interpretation. 													1m
Communication													3m

questions.text: Describe what eye accommodation is. Illustrate this with daily-life examples.															(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Eye accommodation is the ability of the eye to focus on objects at different distances.																	1m
It is brought about by the action of the ciliary muscles, which contract or relax to change the tension in the suspensory ligaments,								1m
thereby changing the curvature of lens for focusing light rays onto the retina.		1m
For example, when we are reading a book (or other suitable examples), we are focusing on a near object.												1m
Ciliary muscles contract. This reduces the tension in the suspensory ligaments and makes them slacken.												1m
Since the lens is elastic, it becomes more convex (thicker) and refracts light more.																	1m
When we are looking at the buildings across the harbour (or other suitable examples), we are focusing on distant objects.									1m
Ciliary muscles relax. This increases the tension in the suspensory ligaments and they become tightened. 												1m
As a result, the lens is pulled. The lens becomes less convex (thinner) and refracts light less.															1m
Communication													3m

questions.text: Describe the structure and functions of the spinal cord.				(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Structure: 
The spinal cord extends from the medulla oblongata of the brain. /
It consists of two regions, the inner region and outer region. / 
The outer region is made up of white matter. /
The inner H-shaped region is made up of grey matter. /
At the centre of the grey matter is the central canal which is filled with cerebrospinal fluid. /
Pairs of spinal nerves arise from the spinal cord. /
The dorsal roots contain sensory neurones which transmit nerve impulses from the receptors to the spinal cord. /
The cell bodies of the sensory neurones group together to form dorsal root 
ganglions. /
The ventral roots contain motor neurones which transmit nerve impulses from the spinal cord to the effectors.

Communication												3m

questions.text: Compare reflex actions and voluntary actions.					(9 marks)
questions.answerText:
Reflex actions involve the spinal cord or brain (mainly medulla oblongata) while voluntary actions always involve the cerebrum.							1m
Reflex actions always involve a receptor while voluntary actions may not involve a receptor.														1m
Reflex actions are not under conscious control while voluntary actions are under conscious control.												1m
Reflex actions are inborn while voluntary actions are not inborn.				1m
In reflex actions, the same stimulus always results in the same response, while in voluntary actions, the same stimulus may result in different responses.			1m
The speed of response in reflex actions is always fast while voluntary actions may be fast or slow depending on the nervous pathway involved and the nature of response.																	1m
Communication													3m

questions.text:
Mary felt dizzy after having a big meal. She went to see a doctor.
The doctor found that a tumour developed in the pancreas of Mary due to uncontrolled division of the cells. The doctor advised Mary to undergo a surgery to remove the affected part of the pancreas. After the surgery, Mary has to reduce the amount of food taken in each meal.

b	Explain why Mary has to reduce the amount of food taken in each meal after the surgery.										(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	The blood glucose level of Mary increased after she had the big meal. This stimulated the pancreas to produce more insulin.						1m
The number of insulin-secreting cells in her pancreas had increased due to uncontrolled cell division. Thus, the amount of insulin produced was larger than the normal amount.												1m
The large amount of insulin caused her blood glucose level to fall to an abnormally low level. Her brain therefore could not obtain enough glucose for metabolism and thus Mary felt dizzy.											1m
b	After the surgery, Mary's pancreas may not produce enough insulin when her blood glucose level is too high. 									1m
Having small meals can prevent too much glucose from absorbing into the blood. This helps prevent her blood glucose level from rising too much.			1m

questions.text: Describe how homeostasis is brought about by negative feedback mechanism.															(9 marks)
questions.answerText:
Negative feedback mechanism results in responses that have opposite effects on the changes in the level of the parameter, so that the level of the parameter can be restored to normal. 													1m
The mechanism involves three components: a receptor, a control centre and an effector. 															1m
The receptor detects changes in the level of the parameter. 				1m
The control centre compares the level of parameter with the set point. 		1m
It is usually part of the nervous system or the endocrine system. 				1m
The control centre sends messages to an effector to initiate a response that has an opposite effect on the original change. 								1m
Communication													3m

questions.text: Explain the roles of the pancreas, liver and body cells in the regulation of blood glucose level.												(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
When the pancreas detects an increase in blood glucose level, it produces more insulin and less glucagon. 												1m
Insulin stimulates liver cells to convert the excess glucose to glycogen. 		1m
The glycogen is then stored in the liver. 								1m
Insulin also stimulates body cells to take in more glucose from the blood. 		1m
As a result, the blood glucose level falls and returns to normal. 				1m
When the pancreas detects a decrease in blood glucose level, it produces more glucagon and less insulin. 											1m
Glucagon stimulates liver cells to convert the stored glycogen to glucose. 		1m
The glucose is then released to the blood. 								1m
As a result, the blood glucose level rises and returns to normal. 				1m
Communication													3m

questions.text: Describe the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis and state the fate of the products.															(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Process of the Calvin cycle:
The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma of chloroplasts.					1m
Carbon dioxide combines with a molecule of a 5-C carbon dioxide acceptor to form two molecules of a 3-C compound.									1m
The 3-C compound is reduced to triose phosphate using energy from ATP and hydrogen from NADPH produced in photochemical reactions.					1m
Two molecules of triose phosphate combine to form one molecule of glucose. 																1m
Some triose phosphate is used to regenerate the 5-C carbon dioxide acceptor using energy from ATP.											1m
Fate of the products:
Glucose acts as the main energy source. /
Glucose is built into starch, which is stored in leaves. /
Starch is broken down to form sucrose, which is transported by the phloem to other parts of the plant. /
Glucose is built into cellulose, which is the major component of cell walls. /
The intermediates of photosynthesis can also be used to synthesize glycerol and fatty acids, which then combine to form lipids. Lipids are used to form cell membranes / stored as energy reserves. /
The intermediates of photosynthesis can also combine with minerals to form amino acids, which then combine to form proteins. Proteins are important for growth and  repair / for the synthesis of enzymes / as the components of cell membranes.
(any 2)													1m x 2
Communication 											3m

questions.text: What is a 'limiting factor'? Explain, with one named factor, the effect of the limiting factor on the rate of photosynthesis. 					(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Meaning of limiting factor:
When a process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is limited by the factor that is in the shortest supply. This factor is called the limiting factor. 				1m
An increase in the value of this factor will lead to an increase in the rate of reaction until some other factors become limiting.									1m
Effects of limiting factors on the rate of photosynthesis:
Light intensity													1m

The rate of photosynthesis increases proportionately with light intensity		1m
as more energy is supplied to the photochemical reactions. 				1m
At high light intensities, other factors become limiting.						1m
OR
Carbon dioxide concentration										1m
At low carbon dioxide concentrations, carbon dioxide is a limiting factor. 		1m
The rate of photosynthesis increases proportionately with carbon dioxide concentration
															1m
because more substrates are supplied to the Calvin cycle. 					1m
At high carbon dioxide concentrations, other factors become limiting.			1m

questions.text: Describe the process of photosynthesis.							(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Photosynthesis occurs in two main stages: photochemical reactions and the Calvin cycle. 													1m
The process of photochemical reactions:
The chlorophyll molecules in the thylakoids of chloroplasts capture light energy. /
Some electrons of the chlorophyll molecules are raised to a higher energy level. /
These excited electrons pass through a series of electron carriers (the electron transport chain) in the thylakoid membrane and release energy gradually. /
Some energy released is used to form ATP by combining a phosphate with ADP (photophosphorylation). /
Some energy is used to split water molecules to form hydrogen and oxygen. /
Hydrogen is accepted by NADP to form NADPH.	 /
Oxygen is released as a gas to the atmosphere. 
(any 3)													1m x 3
The process of the Calvin cycle:
Carbon dioxide combines with a molecule of a 5-C carbon dioxide acceptor to form two molecules of a 3-C compound. /
The 3-C compound is reduced into triose phosphate using energy from ATP and hydrogen from NADPH produced in photochemical reactions. /
Two molecules of triose phosphate combine to form one molecule of glucose. /
Some triose phosphate is used to regenerate the 5-C carbon dioxide acceptor using energy from ATP. 
(any 3)													1m x 3
Communication												3m

questions.text: Explain how the structure of leaves is adapted to obtain raw materials and energy for photosynthesis.											(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Adaptation for obtaining light:
Leaf blade is broad and flat to provide a large surface area for absorbing sunlight. /
Leaf blade is thin to allow light to reach the photosynthetic cells easily. /
Palisade mesophyll consists of tightly packed cells which contain many chloroplasts to allow effective absorption of sunlight. /
Palisade mesophyll is located on the upper side of the leaf to allow effective absorption of sunlight. 
(any 3)													1m x 3
Adaptation for obtaining carbon dioxide: 
Spongy mesophyll consists of loosely packed cells with many air spaces to allow carbon dioxide to diffuse freely inside the leaf. 							1m
Upper and lower epidermis contains numerous stomata to allow gases to diffuse into the leaf. 														1m
Adaptation for obtaining water:
Upper and lower epidermis is covered by waxy cuticle to keep water inside the leaf for photosynthesis.												1m
Each stoma is surrounded by a pair of guard cells to regulate the passage of water vapour into and out of the leaf. 									1m
Midrib and veins contain xylem which allows efficient transport of water into the leaf.
														1m
Communication												3m

questions.text: Describe how ATP is formed in aerobic respiration.				(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Some ATP is formed in glycolysis during the oxidation of triose phosphate to pyruvate.																1m
Some ATP is formed in the Krebs cycle during the conversion of the 6-C compound to the 4-C compound.												1m
NADH is formed during the oxidation of triose phosphate to pyruvate, the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and the conversion of the 6-C compound to the 4-C compound.																1m
FADH is formed during the conversion of the 6-C compound to the 4-C compound.																1m
NADH and FADH lose hydrogen in oxidative phosphorylation. 				1m

Energy is released in the process to form ATP. 							1m

questions.text: Describe the similarities and differences in the processes of photosynthesis and respiration.												(9 marks)

questions.text:
Read the following article and answer the questions.
	Coronary bypass surgery is a treatment for patients with coronary heart disease. During the surgery, the patient is anaesthetized and connected to a heart-lung machine. The heart is then stopped and a section of a large vein from the thigh is used to connect the aorta and coronary artery across the blockage site.
	After the surgery, the patient has to stay in hospital to recover for at least a week. The patient is advised to avoid foods with a high cholesterol level after the surgery.	

a	Describe the cause of coronary heart disease.				(3 marks)
b	Explain why coronary heart disease can be effectively treated with coronary bypass surgery.										(2 marks)
c	What is the function of the heart-lung machine?				(2 marks)
d	Why is the patient advised to avoid foods with a high cholesterol level after the surgery? 											(1 mark)
questions.answerText:
a	Fatty substances like cholesterol in blood deposit within the wall of a coronary artery. A plaque is formed.										1m
The plaque hardens and becomes larger. It narrows the lumen of the artery.	1m
This reduces the amount of blood flowing to the cardiac muscles and causes coronary heart disease.										1m
b	During the surgery, a new route connecting the aorta and coronary artery is made, bypassing the blockage site.									1m
The new pathway allows adequate blood to reach the cardiac muscles.	1m
c	The heart-lung machine is used to pump blood around the body during the surgery. 														1m
Gas exchange also occurs in the machine. 						1m
d	To prevent cholesterol from depositing on the inner wall of the coronary arteries again.													1m

Ten healthy people are fed with the food (the amounts may be different for different foods). The changes in the blood glucose level of them over the next two hours are recorded. The GI value can be calculated by taking the average value of the changes in the blood glucose level of these 10 people comparing to a reference food.

The lipid / protein / dietary fibre content of the food / 
The cooking method (any 2)								1m x 2
e	Diabetics should choose foods with low GI value in everyday diet to prevent a rapid increase in blood glucose level.							1m

questions.text: State the cause of coronary heart disease and discuss how smoking increases the risk of this disease.											(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Cause:
For the heart to work properly, the coronary arteries must supply enough nutrients and oxygen to the cardiac muscles continuously.							1m
If fatty substances like cholesterol in blood deposit within the wall of a coronary artery, a plaque is formed. 												1m
Over time, the plaque hardens and becomes larger. It narrows the lumen of the artery. 															1m
This reduces the amount of blood flowing to the cardiac muscles and causes coronary heart disease. 													1m
How smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease:
Nicotine in cigarette smoke causes constrictions of blood vessels. 			1m
This reduces the amount of blood flowing to the cardiac muscles. 			1m
Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke reduces the oxygen carrying capacity of blood. 																1m 
Less oxygen is supplied to the cardiac muscles. 						1m
Communication													3m

questions.topic: Ch23 · Infectious diseases and disease prevention
questions.text: Give an account on the ways of transmission of infectious diseases from one person to another. Name one disease transmitted by each way.		(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Ways of transmission with examples: (any 4)						2m x 4
By droplets or air:
When patients talk, cough or sneeze, droplets containing pathogens are expelled from the breathing system. Transmission of diseases occurs when these droplets deposit on the mucous membranes of the eyes, nose or mouth of another person. Transmission of diseases may also occur when suspended particles carrying pathogens or fungal spores are inhaled.
e.g. influenza / SARS / measles / tuberculosis
By water or food:
Water or food contaminated with pathogens is ingested.
e.g. cholera / gastroenteritis
By body fluids:
Pathogens in the blood of patients enter the body of another person through wounds, sharing of injection needles, transfusion or during childbirth. Pathogens in semen and vaginal secretion of the patients enter the body of another person during sexual intercourse.
e.g. hepatitis B / AIDS
By vectors:
Pathogens are picked up by some animals and transmitted to new hosts.
e.g. typhus / cholera / malaria / dengue fever
By direct contact:
Pathogens transfer directly when patients are in contact physically with another person.
e.g. athlete's foot / sexually transmitted diseases such as genital herpes
Communication												3m

questions.topic: Ch23 · Infectious diseases and disease prevention
questions.text: Describe the differences between viruses and bacteria as causes of infectious diseases in humans.											(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Viruses can cause diseases only inside cells while bacteria can cause diseases inside or outside cells.													2m
All viruses entering the human body can cause diseases while many bacteria in the human body do not cause diseases.									2m
Viruses cause diseases by disrupting the cellular mechanism or damaging the cell membranes of the host cells, while bacteria cause diseases by producing toxins or enzymes.														2m
Bacterial infections can be treated by antibiotics and sulpha drugs while viral infections cannot.														2m
Communication													3m

questions.answerText:
Mendel's first law of inheritance:
Alleles of each gene are located on a pair of homologous chromosomes and the 	two members of the homologous pair separate during anaphase I.				1m
Each gamete receives one member of the homologous pair and hence its allele.																	1m
Mendel's second law of inheritance:

The members of each homologous pair then separate independently of the 	other pairs of chromosomes during anaphase I.									1m
The separation of alleles for one gene on a pair of homologous chromosomes is therefore independent of the separation of alleles for other genes located on the other chromosomes.													1m

questions.text: Describe the structure of DNA molecules.					(11 marks)

Each nucleotide consists of three parts: a deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. 												1m
There are four types of bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).																1m
Nucleotides are joined between the deoxyribose of one nucleotide and the phosphate group of the next to form a sugar-phosphate backbone.					1m
DNA molecules are double-stranded. 								1m
The two strands run in opposite directions and twist around each other to form a double helix. 														1m
The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between the bases. 		1m
A pairs with T and C pairs with G.									1m

questions.text: Describe the major steps of DNA fingerprinting and discuss the application of DNA fingerprinting in forensic science.							(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
DNA fingerprinting is a technique to identify an individual based on a DNA sample.																1m
It makes use of the difference in the base sequence on the DNA between individuals.																1m
To produce a DNA fingerprint of an individual, DNA is first extracted from the cells of the individual. 													1m
DNA fragments containing selected regions (e.g. highly variable regions) are obtained.																1m
The DNA fragments are separated according to their size using gel electrophoresis.																1m
The pattern of bands obtained after gel electrophoresis is the DNA fingerprint. It is unique to the individual. 											1m
DNA fingerprints can provide evidence on the identities of individuals in court cases. 																1m
The DNA fingerprint produced using the DNA sample collected at the crime scene can be used to compare with that of the suspect. 							1m
If the band patterns match, the sample collected at the crime scene is likely to have come from the suspect. 											1m 
Communication													3m

questions.text:
Darwin and Lamarck proposed their theories to explain the mechanism of evolution. Which of the following is stated in both theories?
A	Variations exist among individuals of the same species.
B	Individuals can develop new characters in response to the environmental changes.
C	The environment selects those individuals with favourable characters to survive.
D	The characters of individuals would be passed on to their offspring.

Evolution of species is likely to be faster in a changing environment than in a stable environment because
A	more individuals are produced in the changing environment.
B	variations among individuals in the changing environment are larger.
C	the environment keeps selecting individuals with different characters in the changing environment.
D	mutations in the changing environment are more frequent.

When the theory of natural selection was first put forward by Darwin, it was 	based on
A	Lamarck's findings.
B	the knowledge of genes and variations.
	C	the results from many controlled experiments.
	D	the observations of the natural world.

In which of the following ways are the explanations for the mechanism of evolution by Darwin and Lamarck similar?
(1)	Evolution involves environmental changes which create variations among individuals.
(2)	Evolution relies on the passing on of characters from parents to offspring.
(3)	Individuals with acquired characters survive and reproduce.
	A	(2) only				B	(1) and (2) only
	C	(1) and (3) only		D	(2) and (3) only

According to Darwin's theory of natural selection, what is the cause of the struggle for existence within a population?
A	variations between individuals 
B	overproduction of offspring
	C	inheritance of favourable characters in offspring
	D	adaptation to the environment

Which of the following supports the theory of natural selection?
A	Selective breeding of domesticated animals can cause species to change.
B	Mice with their tails cut off give birth to offspring with tails.
	C	Offspring produced by sexual reproduction are genetically different.
	D	Giraffes have long necks.

A	Large animals could not cope with environmental changes and became sterile.
B	Environmental changes forced animals to learn tree-climbing skills.
C	Larger tree-climbing mammals reduced their size to cope with environmental changes.
D	Small tree-climbing mammals coped better with environmental changes and survived to produce offspring.

Which of the following processes tends to reduce variety within a population?
A	mutation						B	speciation
	C	natural selection				D	gene flow

Why do bacteria in general evolve more rapidly than plants?
(1)	Bacteria reproduce by binary fission.
	(2)	Bacteria have a shorter life cycle.
(3)	Bacteria mutate more readily.
	A	(1) and (2) only				B	(1) and (3) only
	C	(2) and (3) only				D	(1), (2) and (3)

According to Lamarckism,
(1)	organisms develop new features to meet the needs created by environmental changes.
	(2)	variations already exist among individuals of a species.
	(3)	acquired characters are passed on to offspring.

	B	(1) and (3) only

	A	natural selection.

B	(1) and (3) only

According to Darwin and Wallace, the process of evolution can be explained by
A	heredity.			B	reproduction.

Which of the following are stated in both Lamarck's theory and Darwin's theory of evolution?
(1)	Environmental changes are needed for evolution to occur.

Which of the following is an explanation for the change in the proportion of the two kinds of turtles in the population?

Which of the following comparisons between Lamarck's theory and Darwin's theory of evolution is not correct?

Which of the following concepts are included in the theory of natural selection?

A	all races look alike.

questions.text:
a	Briefly describe what natural selection is.					(2 marks)
b	Darwin illustrated the evolution of the neck of giraffes by his theory of natural selection. According to his theory, explain how the giraffes evolved to become long-necked.									(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	Natural selection is the preservation of favourable characters and the elimination of unfavourable characters in a population.							1m
It allows those organisms with favourable characters to survive and reproduce.																1m
b	The ancestors of modern giraffes had variation in neck length. Some had long necks and some had short necks. 								1m
When there was a shortage of grass,								1m
a long neck became a favourable character for survival.				1m
It allowed the giraffes to get leaves from treetops.					1m
Long-necked giraffes survived and reproduced. They passed on the character of long neck to their offspring.										1m
After many generations, giraffes with long necks predominated in the population. 																1m

questions.text: Describe how isolation leads to the formation of new species. 		(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Isolation is the separation of a population into different groups so that they cannot interbreed. 													1m
There is no gene flow between the two groups. 							1m
Mutations take place within different groups to produce different genetic variations.																	1m
Since the isolated groups may face different environmental conditions, natural selection acts on them in different ways. 										1m
Organisms with favourable characters will be more likely to survive and reproduce. They pass the favourable characters on to their offspring. 						1m
As the environment continually changes, different genetic variations will be selected. 																	1m
After many generations, the isolated groups will have such diverse variation that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring even if they come into contact again. They become different species. 								1m
Communication													3m

questions.text:
The human protein, insulin, is involved in the homeostatic control of blood 
sugar. Most artificially produced human insulin is currently produced by genetically modified bacteria, but several companies are now investigating the possibility of producing human insulin using the safflower plant, a plant which is normally grown for its oil. This method would allow large scale production and, in theory, one large North American farm would be capable of meeting the global demand for insulin.
The first stage in this process would be the isolation and removal of the human insulin gene. Once isolated, the gene is then placed into a vector. One example of such a vector is the bacterium, Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a relatively common soil bacterium that regularly infects plants.
a	Describe how the human insulin gene could be inserted into the bacterium, Agrobacterium tumefaciens.								(4 marks)
The genetically modified bacterium is then allowed to infect a sample of cells extracted from the safflower plant and these infected cells can be grown into mature plants, each being capable of producing human insulin. The human insulin produced by these plants appears to be fully effective in the treatment of diabetes mellitus. However, a patient's blood insulin cannot be raised by simply eating transgenic safflower plants.
b	Suggest why eating safflower plants containing insulin would not result in an increase in the patient's blood insulin levels.				(2 marks)
One possible risk of growing a genetically modified crop in this way is that it might interbreed with wild plants. Pharmaceutical companies try to minimize such risk by growing the crop 'counter-seasonally' to reduce the chances of the insulin gene being transferred to other plants.
c	Suggest what is meant by the term 'counter-seasonally'.		(1 mark)
						CCEA GCE (AS) Biology Module 1 Jun 2009 Q7b-d
questions.answerText:
a	A plasmid obtained from the bacterium and the human insulin gene are cut with the same restriction enzyme. 										1m
The sticky ends allow the plasmid and the human insulin gene to bind together with hydrogen bonds. 										1m
A DNA ligase catalyses the joining of the plasmid and the human insulin gene by helping the formation of covalent bonds. 							1m
A bacterium takes up the plasmid.								1m
b	Insulin is a protein. It will be digested / broken down if it is ingested.		1m
The absorbed amino acids cannot be reassembled into insulin in the body due to the lack of a functional gene.									1m
c	Genetically modified plants flower when other plants are not flowering to reduce the chances of cross-pollination.									1m

questions.text:
Read the following article and answer the questions.
Leukaemia is a kind of cancer. Scientists found that in some patients it is caused by a specific type of translocation mutation.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can be used to detect this mutation for the diagnosis of leukaemia. mRNA is first extracted from the cells of a person who is suspected to have leukaemia. Single-stranded DNA is synthesized using mRNA. 

The DNA is then amplified by PCR. Two different primers are used. Each primer can bind to a region on the DNA or its complementary strand of DNA. The two regions flank the junction where two chromosome segments join in the translocation mutation.

The DNA fragments in the PCR product are then separated by gel electrophoresis. A specific band will appear in the gel only if the person has the mutation.	

a	What is a translocation mutation?							(1 mark)
b	State how mutations may lead to the onset of cancer.			(1 mark)
c	Calculate how many double-stranded DNA molecules would be present in the reaction mixture at the end of cycle 6 of PCR.				(2 marks)
d	Explain why a specific band will appear in the gel only if the person has the translocation mutation in the genome.						(3 marks)
e	Suggest two advantages of using PCR in disease diagnosis.		(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	A translocation mutation is the exchange of segments of chromosomes between non-homologous chromosomes.									1m
b	Mutations in the DNA that controls cell division may lead to uncontrollable division of the cells.												1m
c	2(6-1) 													1m
= 32														1m
d	The translocation mutation brings the segments of chromosomes from two chromosomes together.										1m
If the mutation does occur, the two primers will bind to both the DNA strands in cycle 2 and amplification of the DNA molecule results.					1m
If the mutation does not occur, only one primer will bind to one of the two DNA strands in cycle 2. Amplification of the DNA molecule cannot be carried out.	1m
e	It is a fast method.											1m
Only a small amount of sample is needed.							1m
(or other reasonable answers)

questions.text:

questions.text:
Scientists have produced a GM soya bean plant which is resistant to a herbicide. When farmers apply the herbicide to a field, weeds in the field are killed while the GM soya bean plants remain alive. questions.answerText:

questions.text:

In an attempt to reduce food shortage, some crop plants have been genetically modified so that they can produce a protein toxic to certain insect pests. The protein is normally produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. However, some people argue that the production of the genetically modified (GM) plants is not a solution to food shortage in developing countries and may cause environmental problems.
a	i	When the gene coding for the toxic protein is introduced into plant cells, antibiotic resistance genes are added as well. What is the use of these antibiotic resistance genes?	 					(1 mark)
ii	The use of antibiotic resistance genes in the production of the GM plants has caused concern. Why?						(2 marks)
b	How may the GM plants reduce food shortage?				(1 mark)

Other insect pests may not be killed by the GM plants.					1m Insect pests may become resistant to the toxic protein.				1m

questions.text:

Scientists are developing gene therapy to treat CF. One approach is to supplement the defective gene with a normal one. The normal gene is inserted into a vector. Then the vector carries the gene into the patient's cells.
a	i	Suggest what can be used as a vector in gene therapy.		(1 mark)

a	i	A harmless virus (or other reasonable answers)					1m

questions.answerText:

b	The artificial pacemaker should increase the heart rate.				1m

cardiac muscle so that the muscle cells can respire at a higher rate to release more energy for muscle contractions.								1m

questions.text:
Reed beds which comprise a large number of densely-grown common reed grasses can function as natural wastewater treatment facilities. Common reed grasses are aquatic plants. Their roots grow in submerged soil, while the leaves, flowers and part of the stems grow out of water. Their tissues have air spaces that allow oxygen to travel from the leaves to the roots. As oxygen diffuses out of the roots to the soil, oxygen concentration gradients are set up over short distances. The localized aerobic and anaerobic conditions created favour the growth of many microorganisms which help break down organic waste in wastewater into nitrates and nitrogen gas, etc. The adequate supply of oxygen to the roots also increases the absorption of breakdown products into the plants for growth.

c	If runoff containing a high level of nitrates is used directly in the freshwater habitats in the Hong Kong Wetland Park, algal blooms may occur. Explain why algal blooms can result in the death of aquatic organisms in the freshwater habitats.										(2 marks)
d	Suggest three advantages of using reed beds to treat wastewater in the Hong Kong Wetland Park.									(3 marks)

questions.text:
Read the following article and answer the questions.
Overnight, the small island in the Pacific Ocean becomes famous. A new species of bird has just been discovered by a small team of scientists.
The chief scientist, Dr Smith said, 'We are surprised as the bird is of great use in ecological research.' After five-day work, the team estimated that there are 500 of the birds. 'The birds lose their ability to fly as they are too heavy. They cannot be found elsewhere and no other birds are able to live on the island.' Dr Smith continued.
The governor of the island thanked the team for their effort and announced a new development project. A large pier, roads and hotels will be built in five years. The people on the island welcome the project and look forward to more tourists visiting the rare birds.
However, a local environmental group strongly recommends an immediate conservation programme to protect the birds. They worry that the birds will become extinct soon.	

a	Suggest two possible reasons to explain why the birds can only be found on the island but not in any other places.						(2 marks)
b	Explain why the environmental group worries that the birds will become extinct soon.											(3 marks)
c	The environmental group strongly recommends an immediate conservation programme to protect the birds. State three reasons why the birds should be conserved.											(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	They may feed on food that is present only on the island. /
They may face no / little competition on the island as no other birds are living in the same habitat. /
Natural predators may not be present on the island. (any 2)			1m x 2
b	The tourists coming to the island may disturb the birds. /
Building of the pier, roads and hotels may destroy the birds' habitat. /
The birds may catch diseases from the foreign animals brought to the island by the tourists. /
Predators of the birds may be brought to the island by the tourists. /
Pollution may harm the birds. (any 3)							1m x 3

c	Economic reason: The birds may act as a source of resources, e.g. medicines. /
Ecological reason: The birds feed on some organisms at lower trophic levels. The extinction of the birds disturbs ecological balance. /
Aesthetic reason: People enjoy seeing the birds in their natural habitats. /
Moral reason: The birds have their right to live. (any 3)				1m x 3

questions.text:

'Slash and burn' is one of the methods for people to clear the forest or grassland areas for agriculture and animal farming. Most of the plants in a selected area are cut down, dried and burnt. Crops are then grown on the fertile land. After a few years, the fertility of the soil drops and poor crop growth results. People then move to other areas and the process is repeated.
'Slash and burn' is considered as destructive to the ecology. If only a small number of people using this method, there is sufficient time for the cleared land to recover. But with a larger population, the forest or grassland areas will be destroyed eventually. In modern agriculture, chemical fertilizers are often used to maintain soil fertility.	

a	Why is the land obtained by 'slash and burn' fertile?			(2 marks)

c	State four advantages of conserving a forest ecosystem.		(4 marks)
d	Apart from using chemical fertilizers, suggest two other methods to maintain soil fertility.									(2 marks)

questions.text:
Read the following article and answer the questions.
	Viruses can infect humans and cause diseases. Antiviral drugs can be used to treat viral infections. Some of these drugs work by preventing the entry of the viral nucleic acid into the cells. Some inhibit the uncoating process of the viruses. Others prevent the release of newly synthesized viruses from the infected cells. However, none of these drugs are effective if the viruses remain latent after entering the cells.	

a	Describe the events that would happen after a virus entered the human body.														(4 marks)
b	Suggest one way in which the antiviral drugs prevent the entry of the viruses into the cells.									(1 mark)
c	Explain why preventing the release of newly synthesized viruses can help treat viral infection.										(2 marks)
d	Explain why the drugs stated in the article are not effective if the viruses remain latent.											(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
a	The virus recognizes and attaches to a host cell by binding its surface proteins to specific receptors on the cell membrane of the host cell. Its nucleic acid enters the host cell.													1m
The viral nucleic acid directs the host cell's machinery to produce many copies of the viral nucleic acid and proteins.								1m
Viral nucleic acids and proteins assemble into new viruses.				1m
New viruses burst the host cell and they are released.					1m
b	The drugs block the receptors on the cell membrane of the cells / block the surface proteins of the viruses that bind to receptors. 
(or other reasonable answers)									1m
c	The new viruses synthesized have to be released from the infected cells before they can infect other cells of the same host.							1m
Preventing the release of viruses can stop the viruses from spreading inside the body.														1m
d	All the antiviral drugs stated in the article target on the processes in the multiplication of the viruses. 									1m
If the viruses remain latent, those processes would not occur. 			1m

															1m

															1m
